subject: PSHE
title: Reporting concerns and seeking help
outcome: Know how to report concerns and seek help.
credit: Lesson resource · CC BY-NC-SA 4.0: free for classroom use, share and adapt with credit, no resale
definition: A concern is something that may affect a person's safety or wellbeing. A person can ask for help even if they are not sure. They do not need proof or a severe problem first.
concerns: A worry that lasts, repeated unkind replies, private details shared without consent, or a request that makes someone feel unsafe can be concerns. No unkind words or private details are shown in this lesson. A person can report a concern for someone else too.
supports: A teacher, teaching assistant or safeguarding lead can listen and use the school help route.
A parent or carer, or another safe adult, can listen and help find support.
Can discuss health concerns and suitable care.
Can listen and give advice. Ask staff to help find a route suited to the person's age and need.
report_steps: Stop replying or sharing if something online causes concern. Move away from it if needed.
Tell trusted school staff or another trusted adult privately. Use words, a note, HELP or a usual aid.
With adult help, use a report tool on the item or account where suitable. Say which rule or problem fits, using facts. Block or mute may help too.
Do not forward, download or copy harmful or private content to prove it. Let trusted staff guide any safe record through school procedure.
Ask what will happen next and when to check back. If the first adult is unavailable or help is not enough, ask another trusted adult.
what_next: An adult should listen, take the concern seriously and explain the next step in a way the person can understand. They may need to share information with the safeguarding lead or other people who can help keep someone safe. They cannot promise a secret. A report tool may send a reply or check the content; it may take time and may not resolve the concern. The learner can keep asking for adult help. No fixed result or time is promised.
help: Use a trusted adult or school staff in private. Point to HELP, write a request or say Can we talk in private. Ask another trusted adult if the first is busy or help is not enough. Outside school, a trusted adult can help contact a family doctor or a suitable helpline. For an immediate safety concern, get adult help at once and follow the urgent help route; do not wait for an online reply.
step_out: Before teaching, agree a discreet HELP or PAUSE signal and the familiar supervised place and route. Staff acknowledge the signal quietly and keep adult support. No public reason is needed. Offer a neutral task, supported return or private catch-up. Do not send a learner away alone.
safeguarding: Any disclosure goes to the safeguarding lead through school procedure. Listen calmly, reassure, do not probe, investigate or promise secrecy. Follow urgent school procedures for immediate concerns. Keep real concerns and identifying details in the separate safeguarding record, not learning evidence. A pupil unable to identify a trusted adult is supported privately, not pressed.
private_card: My three people is an optional private card for three support roles, never names. Any or all spaces may stay blank; use an invented learner or pass. Keep it with the pupil. Do not collect, photograph, display, compare or copy it into evidence. Three filled spaces are not a success test. An agreed scribe returns it to the pupil.

cases.title: A repeated unkind reply
cases.text: A young person sees repeated unkind replies about a craft task in an invented group chat. No unkind words are shown. They stop replying and want help.
cases.clue: Repeated unkind replies may affect wellbeing.
cases.ask: Can we talk in private? I need help with unkind replies.
cases.help: School staff can listen, follow the school route and help use report or block tools. The learner can ask what comes next and when to check back.

cases.title: A shared routine note
cases.text: A young person learns that a note with their routine was shared online without asking. No routine details are shown. They want help to limit the sharing.
cases.clue: Private routine details shared without consent can be a concern.
cases.adult: A trusted adult or school staff
cases.ask: Can we talk in private? A routine note was shared and I need help.
cases.help: An adult can help use reporting tools and the school route. The learner should not send copies to other people. They can ask for a next step and check-back time.

cases.title: A worry about a new routine
cases.text: A young person has felt worried about a new routine for a while. It makes daily tasks hard. They want to tell an adult but are not sure how to start.
cases.clue: A lasting worry that makes daily life hard may need support.
cases.adult: A trusted adult, school staff or a family doctor
cases.ask: Can we talk in private? I am finding this routine hard and would like help.
cases.help: A trusted adult can listen and help plan support or find suitable care. They explain the next step. A suitable helpline may also help; ask staff to find an age-appropriate route.

routes.Supported: Choose either task. Keep the short bank, starter and visible model. Offer two support roles if needed. Point, type, use a usual aid or exact scribe and readback. Separate content cues from usual access.
routes.Independent: Choose either task. Explain the concern, a fitting adult role and private opener. Give a safe action and what to ask about next. Keep usual aids and the model.
routes.Aspire: Choose either task. Compare school and outside support. Adapt the route if the first adult is busy or a report tool does not help. Explain why proof or a secrecy promise is not needed. No personal account required.

success: Recognise a concern in an invented case without needing proof.
Choose school and outside support by role and give a private opener.
Explain a safe report step, what may happen next and how to ask again.

hinge.question: The learner is unsure if a shared routine note is a concern. What should they do?
choices: A Wait until they have proof.
B Ask a trusted adult privately now.
C Share copies with more people.
D Keep it secret if someone asks.
hinge.parallel: The first adult is busy. A Ask another trusted adult through the agreed route. B Give up and keep the concern secret.
hinge.rule: Check privately. B or safe equivalent with a reason: proceed. A means proof is wrongly required; C spreads private content; D accepts secrecy. Re-model with the fictional case and use parallel A. Pass or no response is unobserved; revisit with support, not a failure label.

timing: Settle, agree private help and pause; choose a concern or explain why help is valid.
Define concern and school/outside support types; report even when unsure.
Model A with stop, tell, supported report and what next. Match steps or improve advice.
Check no proof or secrecy needed. Choose task and response mode.
Report map B or support note C; include optional private three-role card.
Use shared checks; one next step and pupil response.
Explain a next route or correct a reporting myth. Confirm help.
where_this_leads: This helps me raise a concern and ask for support in school, a group or future work.
marking: Retain actual fictional learning evidence, usual access and content prompts. Set one NS and allow a reply in the pupil's own colour or usual mode. E only for actual saved work. R only after Voice, Audience, one NS and an actual pupil response. Offer to the Communication portfolio; staff confirm any mapping. Personal support cards and real concerns are not learning evidence.

paragraphs: Staff answers and cover notes
Exact outcome
Know how to report concerns and seek help.
Meaning and concerns

A concern is something that may affect a person's safety or wellbeing. A person can ask for help even if they are not sure. They do not need proof or a severe problem first. A worry that lasts, repeated unkind replies, private details shared without consent, or a request that makes someone feel unsafe can be concerns. No unkind words or private details are shown in this lesson. A person can report a concern for someone else too.
School staff
A teacher, teaching assistant or safeguarding lead can listen and use the school help route.
A trusted adult outside school
A parent or carer, or another safe adult, can listen and help find support.
A family doctor
Can discuss health concerns and suitable care.
A suitable helpline
Can listen and give advice. Ask staff to help find a route suited to the person's age and need.
Safe online reporting
Stop replying or sharing if something online causes concern. Move away from it if needed.
Tell trusted school staff or another trusted adult privately. Use words, a note, HELP or a usual aid.
With adult help, use a report tool on the item or account where suitable. Say which rule or problem fits, using facts. Block or mute may help too.
Do not forward, download or copy harmful or private content to prove it. Let trusted staff guide any safe record through school procedure.
Ask what will happen next and when to check back. If the first adult is unavailable or help is not enough, ask another trusted adult.

Fictional answers and checks
A A repeated unkind reply

Repeated unkind replies may affect wellbeing. School staff can listen, follow the school route and help use report or block tools. The learner can ask what comes next and when to check back. Opener: Can we talk in private? I need help with unkind replies. School staff can help in school; a trusted adult outside school can listen and help find support. Accept other fitting safe roles and reasons.
B A shared routine note

Private routine details shared without consent can be a concern. An adult can help use reporting tools and the school route. The learner should not send copies to other people. They can ask for a next step and check-back time. Opener: Can we talk in private? A routine note was shared and I need help. School staff can help in school; a trusted adult outside school can listen and help find support. Accept other fitting safe roles and reasons.
C A worry about a new routine

A lasting worry that makes daily life hard may need support. A trusted adult can listen and help plan support or find suitable care. They explain the next step. A suitable helpline may also help; ask staff to find an age-appropriate route. Opener: Can we talk in private? I am finding this routine hard and would like help. School staff can help in school; a trusted adult outside school can listen and help find support. Accept other fitting safe roles and reasons.
Equal demand

Map B and note C both show concern, school and outside roles, private opener, safe action, possible next step and fallback. For C, include a general online report step learnt from A, without turning the worry into an online event. A map needs no art skill and a note needs no extra length.
Main and parallel hinge

Main B. A wrongly requires proof. C spreads private content. D accepts secrecy. Re-model then use parallel A: ask another trusted adult through the agreed route. A pass is unobserved. Check privately with the learner usual mode.
Misconceptions and repair

A learner may ask even if unsure. Privacy means a discreet conversation, not a secrecy promise. Reporting may take time or not resolve a concern, so adult support and asking again remain valid. Never blame a person if harm occurs or tools do not work.
Evidence and safe delivery
Judgement

Judge concern knowledge and a safe help route from the fictional response. Retain partial evidence and actual prompts. Usual aids, typing and exact scribing do not supply the learner thinking. Log adult answer choices or models as content help. Do not judge personal wellbeing, conduct or safety.
Review and exit

Improve A report always fixes it at once. A report may take time or fail to solve it, so ask trusted adults again. Exit may give a fallback or correct the proof myth. The self-check is about learning only.
What may happen next

An adult should listen, take the concern seriously and explain the next step in a way the person can understand. They may need to share information with the safeguarding lead or other people who can help keep someone safe. They cannot promise a secret. A report tool may send a reply or check the content; it may take time and may not resolve the concern. The learner can keep asking for adult help. No fixed result or time is promised.
Private three role card

My three people is an optional private card for three support roles, never names. Any or all spaces may stay blank; use an invented learner or pass. Keep it with the pupil. Do not collect, photograph, display, compare or copy it into evidence. Three filled spaces are not a success test. An agreed scribe returns it to the pupil.
Feedback

Retain actual fictional learning evidence, usual access and content prompts. Set one NS and allow a reply in the pupil's own colour or usual mode. E only for actual saved work. R only after Voice, Audience, one NS and an actual pupil response. Offer to the Communication portfolio; staff confirm any mapping. Personal support cards and real concerns are not learning evidence.
Private help

Use a trusted adult or school staff in private. Point to HELP, write a request or say Can we talk in private. Ask another trusted adult if the first is busy or help is not enough. Outside school, a trusted adult can help contact a family doctor or a suitable helpline. For an immediate safety concern, get adult help at once and follow the urgent help route; do not wait for an online reply.
Discreet step out

Before teaching, agree a discreet HELP or PAUSE signal and the familiar supervised place and route. Staff acknowledge the signal quietly and keep adult support. No public reason is needed. Offer a neutral task, supported return or private catch-up. Do not send a learner away alone.
Safeguarding

Any disclosure goes to the safeguarding lead through school procedure. Listen calmly, reassure, do not probe, investigate or promise secrecy. Follow urgent school procedures for immediate concerns. Keep real concerns and identifying details in the separate safeguarding record, not learning evidence. A pupil unable to identify a trusted adult is supported privately, not pressed.
Invented concerns and support roles
All stories are made up. No unkind words or private details are shown. Use these stories for class work. No real story is needed.
A A repeated unkind reply
A young person sees repeated unkind replies about a craft task in an invented group chat. No unkind words are shown. They stop replying and want help.
B A shared routine note
A young person learns that a note with their routine was shared online without asking. No routine details are shown. They want help to limit the sharing.
C A worry about a new routine
A young person has felt worried about a new routine for a while. It makes daily tasks hard. They want to tell an adult but are not sure how to start.
Who could help
Reporting and what may happen next
Step 1
Stop replying or sharing if something online causes concern. Move away from it if needed.
Step 2
Tell trusted school staff or another trusted adult privately. Use words, a note, HELP or a usual aid.
Step 3
With adult help, use a report tool on the item or account where suitable. Say which rule or problem fits, using facts. Block or mute may help too.
Step 4
Do not forward, download or copy harmful or private content to prove it. Let trusted staff guide any safe record through school procedure.
Step 5
Ask what will happen next and when to check back. If the first adult is unavailable or help is not enough, ask another trusted adult.
After telling an adult
The adult should listen, take the concern seriously and explain the next step. They may share it with people who can help keep someone safe. They cannot promise a secret.
After an online report

The report tool may send a reply or check the content. It may take time or not solve the concern. Ask trusted adults again if help is not enough. For an urgent safety concern, get adult help at once; do not wait for an online reply.
Model A

Repeated unkind replies may affect wellbeing. School staff can listen, follow the school route and help use report or block tools. The learner can ask what comes next and when to check back. They could ask: Can we talk in private? I need help with unkind replies.

Ask another trusted adult through the agreed route. Ask what will happen next and when to check back.
Keep this card. Do not hand it in. You do not have to show or explain it. Add no real worry, health or account details.
Staff note: support blank spaces without pressing. Do not collect, photograph, display, compare or copy this card. Any disclosure goes to the safeguarding lead through school procedure.

paragraphs: Words for reporting and help
Use these words with the invented stories. No real concern or account is needed.
Concern
Something that may affect safety or wellbeing. A person can ask for help even if unsure.
Report
Tell someone about a concern so they can help with a safe next step.
Trusted adult
An adult a person feels safe asking for help. They may need to share a concern with people who can help.
Report tool
A tool that flags a concern about a post or account. An adult can help use it. It may not solve the concern.
Private
Away from the group. It does not mean a promise to keep a concern secret.
Check back
Ask about the next step or return if more help is needed.
A private opener

Can we talk in private? I would like help.
If one adult is busy or help is not enough, ask another trusted adult.
A model
A learner can stop replying, tell trusted school staff and ask for help with report tools. They can ask what comes next. They do not need proof before asking.
Your usual route
Point, use an aid, type or ask for an exact scribe. The adult reads back quietly so you can correct it. You may pass or use the agreed supported pause.

Reporting concerns and seeking help

Thread tags: SMSC S/So; British Values IL/MR. Other tags not claimed.
Exact outcome
Know how to report concerns and seek help.
GROW Weekly Spring row 68 C68. Exact outcome checked. Owner supplies the date, period and group. This is a formative lesson.
Purpose

Spot a concern in the story. Choose a school support role and an outside support role. Give a private way to ask. Explain a safe action, what may happen next and how to ask again. For an online step, use your story or the online model A. All scenes are invented, mild and offline. Do not ask for a real concern or account.
Cover preparation

Read Staff Answers. Prepare books, printed Support Cards, glossary and usual aids. Offer the typed Evidence Sheet if useful. Agree the private help and supervised pause route with an available adult before teaching. Follow the same cases and choices if covering.
Forty minute sequence
Total 40 minutes. Processing time and short quiet pauses sit inside these phases. Choices B and C share one task period. The private card is optional, not an extra assessed task.
Where this leads
This helps me raise a concern and ask for support in school, a group or future work.
Teaching and response routes
Starter choices
Choose whether a private note shared without asking could be a concern. Or explain why a person may ask for help even if unsure. Use the invented learner only.
Input

A concern is something that may affect a person's safety or wellbeing. A person can ask for help even if they are not sure. They do not need proof or a severe problem first. A worry that lasts, repeated unkind replies, private details shared without consent, or a request that makes someone feel unsafe can be concerns. No unkind words or private details are shown in this lesson. A person can report a concern for someone else too.
Model A

A young person sees repeated unkind replies about a craft task in an invented group chat. No unkind words are shown. They stop replying and want help. Repeated unkind replies may affect wellbeing. School staff can listen, follow the school route and help use report or block tools. The learner can ask what comes next and when to check back. They could ask: Can we talk in private? I need help with unkind replies.
Guided choices

Match Stop replying then tell a trusted adult to a safe report route. Or improve Wait for proof before asking. Model asking now, then reduce answer cues while keeping the visible model and usual aids.
Two equal main choices

Choose report map B or support note C. Both show the concern, school and outside roles, private opener, safe action, possible next step and a fallback. A map may be a list; a note needs no extra length. Both use books, typing, aids or exact scribing. No public talk or compulsory role play.
Supported

Choose either task. Keep the short bank, starter and visible model. Offer two support roles if needed. Point, type, use a usual aid or exact scribe and readback. Separate content cues from usual access.
Independent
Choose either task. Explain the concern, a fitting adult role and private opener. Give a safe action and what to ask about next. Keep usual aids and the model.
Aspire

Choose either task. Compare school and outside support. Adapt the route if the first adult is busy or a report tool does not help. Explain why proof or a secrecy promise is not needed. No personal account required.
Private keep card

My three people is an optional private card for three support roles, never names. Any or all spaces may stay blank; use an invented learner or pass. Keep it with the pupil. Do not collect, photograph, display, compare or copy it into evidence. Three filled spaces are not a success test. An agreed scribe returns it to the pupil. Offer it within individual work. Assess the fictional task without looking at the card.

Response modes

Books are the first route. Evidence Sheet page 2 offers Type instead for both choices. Point, draw, use a usual aid or exact scribe. Read back quietly and allow correction. Keep reading and language aids. Plan in any language. No public questioning.
Prompt ladder

Point to the place or instruction. Ask a short private question. Rephrase. Offer a scaffold or choice. Model the first step only, then return the task. Allow time. Record answer cues apart from usual access.
Checks and planned access
Main private hinge

The learner is unsure if a shared routine note is a concern. What should they do? A Wait until they have proof. B Ask a trusted adult privately now. C Share copies with more people. D Keep it secret if someone asks. Check privately. B or safe equivalent with a reason: proceed. A means proof is wrongly required; C spreads private content; D accepts secrecy. Re-model with the fictional case and use parallel A. Pass or no response is unobserved; revisit with support, not a failure label.
Parallel check

The first adult is busy. A Ask another trusted adult through the agreed route. B Give up and keep the concern secret. Correct A. Another adult can help; the person need not give up. A pass is unobserved.
Questions in private
F Who could the story learner tell? M Why can they ask without proof? H What if a report tool or first adult does not help? Use words, note, pointing or usual aid. No public questioning.
Misconceptions
Proof is not needed before asking for help. A private talk does not mean secrecy: adults may need to share a safety concern. Report and block tools do not guarantee a result. Adult help can continue.
Planned adaptations

Cognition and Learning: one part at a time, visible model and short choices. Communication and Interaction: wait time, aid, typing or exact scribe with quiet readback. SEMH: predictable mild cases, private response, pass, neutral task and supervised pause. Sensory and Physical: clear print, comfortable position and usual aids. EAL: explain key words and plan in any language.
TA focus

Input: model A and support roles. Guided work: offer a step match or advice repair. Independent: check chosen work privately, record actual aids and answer cues, acknowledge pause signals and keep supervision. Do not fill missing answers or press for a personal report.

An adult should listen, take the concern seriously and explain the next step in a way the person can understand. They may need to share information with the safeguarding lead or other people who can help keep someone safe. They cannot promise a secret. A report tool may send a reply or check the content; it may take time and may not resolve the concern. The learner can keep asking for adult help. No fixed result or time is promised.
Evidence cover and private support
Evidence judgement

Use fictional work only. Check concern, school and outside roles, opener, safe action, possible next step and fallback. Keep partial work and record actual prompts. A pass is unobserved. A story answer does not prove real help seeking or personal safety. The private three-role card is not evidence.
Review and exit

Use shared checks or improve A report always fixes the problem at once. A report may take time or not solve it; trusted adult help can continue. Set one precise NS and retain the reply. Exit: give a next route or correct You need proof before asking. The learning self-check is Ready to explain / With a prompt / Need another example. It does not rate wellbeing.

R only after Voice, Audience, one NS and an actual pupil response. Offer to the Communication portfolio; staff confirm any mapping. Personal support cards and real concerns are not learning evidence.
Non specialist cover

Use only the supplied definitions and cases. If display or typing fails, read cards with a book, aid or scribe. No phone, internet, real post or live report is needed. Do not ask learners to open, save, copy, download or forward concerning content. Staff decide safe recording through school procedures. Never promise secrecy, removal, an outcome or a fixed response time.

Use a trusted adult or school staff in private. Point to HELP, write a request or say Can we talk in private. Ask another trusted adult if the first is busy or help is not enough. Outside school, a trusted adult can help contact a family doctor or a suitable helpline. For an immediate safety concern, get adult help at once and follow the urgent help route; do not wait for an online reply.

Safeguarding

Any disclosure goes to the safeguarding lead through school procedure. Listen calmly, reassure, do not probe, investigate or promise secrecy. Follow urgent school procedures for immediate concerns. Keep real concerns and identifying details in the separate safeguarding record, not learning evidence. A pupil unable to identify a trusted adult is supported privately, not pressed.
